main_text.p: not properly remit sin, but did declare and certify that it was remitted by God; so that the absolution, received from man, is nothing else than if he should say, Behold, my son, I certify thee that thy sins are forgiven thee, I pronounce unto thee that thou hast God favourable unto thee; and whatsoever Christ in baptism and in his gospel hath promised unto us, he doth now declare and promise unto thee by me. Of this shalt thou have me to be a witness: go in peace, and in quiet of conscience." But jam hoc tempore the case is altered: these things must be purged out of Ferusq as erroneous; the opinion of the old doctors must give place to the sentence of the new fathers of Trent. And so we are come at length to the end of this long question; in the handling whereof I have spent the more time, by reason our priests do make this faculty of pardoning men's sins to be one of the most principal parts of their occupation, and the particular discovery thereof is not ordinarily by the writers of our side so much insisted upon.
sit, tibi nunc per me annunciat et promittit. Jo. Ferus, lib. 2. comment. in Matt. cap. 9. edit. Mogunt. ann. 1559.
q Fer. in Matt. edit. Antverp. ann. 1559, 1570, &c.
